## What This Page Does

Every call to one of the estimators in `qte.distributional_did` returns four aggregations of the
same cell-level estimates: `res.group_time` holds them as they are, `res.group` averages over the
periods of a treatment group, `res.event_study` aligns them by time since treatment, and
`res.overall` reduces them to a single number. This page takes them apart, one section per
aggregation.

The examples use changes-in-changes throughout; nothing below depends on which estimator produced
the cells, so the same four aggregations are available from the other three. The estimators
themselves, and the data, are described in [Distributional Difference-in-Differences](did.qmd).

{{< include _setup-did.qmd >}}

## The Data and the Estimates

The two cells below load the demonstration panel and estimate changes-in-changes on it. They repeat
what the other page does, since this page has to be read on its own.

```{python}
#| label: lst-data
from qte.datasets import load_mpdta

panel = load_mpdta().with_columns(
    pl.col("first.treat").replace(0, float("inf")).alias("group")
)
print(f"{panel.height:,} county-year observations for {panel['countyreal'].n_unique()} counties")
```

```{python}
#| label: lst-estimate
from qte.distributional_did import estimate_changes_in_changes_effects

with timer("changes-in-changes"):
    cic = estimate_changes_in_changes_effects(
        panel,
        "lemp",
        "group",
        "year",
        "countyreal",
        qs=QS,
        bootstrap_config=BOOTSTRAP,
    )
```

## The Cells

For every treatment group and period the estimator compares that period with a pre-treatment period
and constructs the counterfactual distribution for the treated group afresh. Each such comparison is
one cell, and the three aggregations below are all built from them: `res.group_time` keeps the cells
as they are, one row per cell and quantile, and the other three average them in different ways.

Cells whose period precedes the treatment are placebos: the estimator is applied to a period in
which nobody was treated yet, so the effects there should be close to zero. With the default base
period (`BasePeriod.UNIVERSAL`) every cell compares to the period just before treatment, so a group
treated in 2007 contributes placebo cells at 2003 to 2006.

## By Treatment Group: `group`

Averaging a group's cells over time gives one estimate per treatment group — the effect of being
treated from that year onwards, on average over the periods in which the group is treated. The
weights are equal within a group, and they sum to one, so each group's estimate is a simple average
over its own post-treatment periods.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-group
cic.group.tabulate(quantiles=QS)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-group
#| fig-cap: "Changes-in-changes, aggregated by treatment group."
show_chart(cic.group.plot())
```

## By Time Since Treatment: `event_study`

The event study reorders the cells by the event time $e = t - g$, so that cells from different
groups but the same distance from treatment line up: the effect at $e = 0$ pools the periods in
which each group is first treated, $e = 1$ the period after, and so on. Negative event times are the
placebos.

The weights are not equal across groups here. At each event time the groups that contribute a cell
are weighted by their number of counties and renormalized, which is why a group contributes to a
different number of event times depending on how many periods it is observed for — 2004 spans $e$
from $-4$ to $3$, while 2007 spans $-4$ to $0$.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-event-study
cic.event_study.tabulate(quantiles=QS)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-event-study
#| fig-cap: "Changes-in-changes by event time; negative event times are placebo cells."
show_chart(cic.event_study.plot())
```

Which cells exist depends on the base period. With `BasePeriod.VARYING` the placebo cells compare to
the immediately preceding period rather than to the period before treatment, which shifts every
negative event time by one and leaves the post-treatment estimates untouched.

```{python}
#| label: lst-varying
from qte.distributional_did import BasePeriod

with timer("base period"):
    cic_varying = estimate_changes_in_changes_effects(
        panel,
        "lemp",
        "group",
        "year",
        "countyreal",
        qs=QS,
        base_period=BasePeriod.VARYING,
        bootstrap_config=BOOTSTRAP,
    )
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-varying
comparison = (
    cic.event_study.att.filter(pl.col("event_study_period") >= 0)
    .select(
        pl.col("event_study_period").alias("Event time"),
        pl.col("effect").alias("Universal base"),
    )
    .join(
        cic_varying.event_study.att.filter(pl.col("event_study_period") >= 0).select(
            pl.col("event_study_period").alias("Event time"),
            pl.col("effect").alias("Varying base"),
        ),
        on="Event time",
    )
)
(
    GT(comparison)
    .tab_header(
        title="Post-treatment effects under the two base periods",
        subtitle="Only the placebo cells, which are not shown, depend on the choice.",
    )
    .fmt_number(["Universal base", "Varying base"], decimals=4)
)
```

## A Single Number: `overall`

The overall aggregation reduces the cells to one estimate. Groups are weighted by their number of
units — here the number of counties, so 20, 40 and 131 — and within a group the post-treatment
periods are weighted equally. The result is therefore the size-weighted average of the three
estimates in the group table.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-overall
cic.overall.tabulate(quantiles=QS)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-overall
#| fig-cap: "Changes-in-changes, overall aggregation."
show_chart(cic.overall.plot())
```

```{python}
#| label: lst-check
n = panel.unique("countyreal").group_by("group").len().rename({"len": "counties"}).sort("group")
weighted = (
    cic.group.att.select(pl.col("treatment_group").cast(pl.Float64).alias("group"), "effect")
    .join(n, on="group")
    .select(
        (pl.col("effect") * pl.col("counties")).sum() / pl.col("counties").sum()
    )
    .item()
)
print(f"size-weighted average of the group estimates: {weighted:.6f}")
print(f"overall aggregation:                           {cic.overall.att['effect'][0]:.6f}")
```

## What the Weights Do

@tbl-weights spells the weights out for this panel. A group's share is its number of counties over
all treated counties; that share is then split equally over the group's post-treatment periods,
which gives the weight each cell receives in the overall aggregation.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-weights
post_cells = (
    panel.select("group", "year")
    .unique()
    .filter(pl.col("year") >= pl.col("group"))
    .group_by("group")
    .agg(pl.col("year").len().alias("periods"))
)
weights = (
    n.join(post_cells, on="group")
    .with_columns(share=pl.col("counties") / pl.col("counties").sum())
    .with_columns(weight=pl.col("share") / pl.col("periods"))
    .select(
        pl.col("group").cast(pl.Int64).alias("Group"),
        "counties",
        "share",
        "periods",
        "weight",
    )
    .rename(
        {
            "counties": "Counties",
            "share": "Group share",
            "periods": "Treated periods",
            "weight": "Weight per cell",
        }
    )
)
(GT(weights).tab_header(title="Aggregation weights").fmt_number(decimals=4))
```

Two things follow from aggregating distributions rather than numbers.

The average effect is an average of the cells' average effects, so the check above goes through
exactly. The quantile treatment effects are not: the aggregation averages the cells' counterfactual
_distributions_ — each evaluated on a common grid of outcomes — and only then inverts the result to
get quantiles. The reported quantile effect at a given quantile is therefore not the weighted
average of the cells' quantile effects at that quantile, and it is the reason the aggregated
quantiles cannot be reproduced from the tables above by hand.

The placebos enter no aggregation other than the event study. `res.overall` and `res.group` use only
post-treatment cells, so a badly behaved placebo shows up in the event-study figure and not in the
headline number.
